children: said its drug plozasiran reduced rates of acute pancreatitis, a sudden inflammation of the pancreas, by 78% compared with placebo in a pooled analysis of two late-stage studies. The company also reported early results showing an experimental treatment lowered both cholesterol and triglycerides, another type of fat in the blood.
The findings could support plozasiran’s commercial prospects and further development of Arrowhead’s

cardiovascular drug pipeline. Shares have fallen 12% year to date. Investors will need to weigh the reported benefits against blood-sugar concerns and the limited evidence available for the earlier-stage treatment.

The SHASTA-3 and SHASTA-4 studies enrolled 757 adults with severely elevated triglycerides who received plozasiran or placebo every three months. Among participants who had experienced pancreatitis within the preceding five years, plozasiran reduced the rate of subsequent attacks by 91% compared with placebo, the company reported at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

Health problems arising during treatment occurred in 73% of participants in both groups. Worsening blood-sugar control was reported in 14% of plozasiran recipients versus 8.7% of placebo recipients. Three deaths in the treatment group were assessed as unrelated to the drug.

Separately, a longer-term extension study found a median triglyceride reduction of 76% after up to three years of plozasiran treatment in patients with familial chylomicronemia syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that causes extremely high blood-fat levels. The extension lacked a concurrent placebo group, limiting comparisons.

experimental ARO-DIMER-PA treatment produced average reductions in LDL, or “bad” cholesterol, of up to 65% and median triglyceride reductions of up to 78% after one dose. The drug uses RNA interference to reduce production of two liver proteins involved in controlling blood fats. These interim results came from small dose groups and were measured against starting levels without adjusting for placebo results.

All 21 participants receiving ARO-DIMER-PA reported health problems during follow-up, most commonly injection-site redness. One experienced severe fainting, although no events were classified as serious. Larger, longer studies are needed to establish safety, dosing and whether the treatment reduces heart attacks or other cardiovascular events.

title: Arrowhead reports lower pancreatitis rates, early cholesterol drug results
